newsitem.title: USA: Stock prices sharply mixed; blue chips hurt by fear of Fed.
newsitem.headline: Stock prices sharply mixed; blue chips hurt by fear of Fed.

text.p: Stock ended sharply mixed Thursday, with blue chips dogged by the prospect that the Federal Reserve will boost interest rates as early as next week and the secondary market led higher by a rebound in technology shares.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed 57.40 points lower at 6,820.28, while the Nasdaq Composite index rose 9.97 to 1,259.26. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,526 to 949 on active volume of 496 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
While investors were selling interest-rate sensitive blue chip stocks, they were also opting to seek out bargains elsewhere.
One beneficiary was the battered technology sector, whose recent woes have produced a double-digit correction over the last two months.
"We passed the 10 percent correction level yesterday and that seems to be a magical level that brings out the bargain hunters," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.
Some analysts said a key measure will be whether the spark of life that emerged from the technology sector gains momentum in the coming sessions.

"The techs are putting in what appears to be a pretty good bounce," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "If the techs can stabilise, the primary market won't be far behind."
Investors also turned to the bond market, which was wobbled early by comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, only to rebound sharply later in the day.
The 30-year Treasury gained 12/32, lowering its yield to 6.96 percent from 6.99 percent on Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Greenspan, who in testimony to Congress spoke of the need for the Fed to act "promptly - ideally pre-emptively" in its fight against inflation, heightened Wall Street's expectations of an interest rate increase at the March 25 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
The recent drop in bonds has lifted their yields high enough to make them compete with stocks.

"A lot of people think that if the Fed tightens, it's already priced into the bond market," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross. "That makes bonds attractive, especially when you consider there's no driving inflation in the economy."

The story was far different for tobacco stocks, which toppled on news that cigarette maker Liggett Group Inc. was close to announcing a settlement of anti-smoking litigation with attorneys general in several states.

Sources familiar with talks between the states and Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group Ltd., said the settlement would include an offer by Liggett to turn over potentially damaging documents about the entire industry.
Shares in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. fell 3/4 to 31-1/2 and Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard Tobacco Co., sank 2-1/4 to 98-1/2. Brooke Group rose 5/8 to 4-7/8.
Looming on Friday is the so-called "triple witching" expiration of options, index options and index futures, an event that invariably adds volatility.
Among other individual issues, Unisource Worldwide Inc. fell 3-3/4 to 16 after warning that its fiscal second-quarter earnings would be below analysts' estimates.
U.S. Bancorp jumped 6-7/8 to 55-1/8 after agreeing to be acquired by First Bank System Inc. for $59 per share in stock. First Bank fell 2-3/4 to 75-1/2.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 3.12 points to 782.65. The American Stock Exchange index was off 0.24 at 591.55.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.81 to 411.78. The average share was down 19 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,453.852, down 14.720, or 0.20 percent.
